message.content:
Here’s a quick snapshot of some of the most celebrated composers who have made their mark in the United States—spanning classical, film, and popular music:

| Composer | Era / Genre | Notable Works / Contributions |
|----------|-------------|--------------------------------|
| **Aaron Copland** (1900‑1990) | Classical | “Appalachian Spring,” “Rodeo,” “Fanfare for the Common Man.” Known for his distinctly “American” sound. |
| **Leonard Bernstein** (1918‑1990) | Classical / Broadway | “West Side Story,” “Candide,” “On the Town.” A charismatic conductor and educator. |
| **Philip Glass** (born 1937) | Minimalism | “Einstein on the Beach,” “Glassworks.” Pioneered repetitive structures in contemporary classical music. |
| **John Williams** (born 1942) | Film | Scores for *Star Wars*, *Indiana Jones*, *Jurassic Park*, *Harry Potter* series. One of the most recognizable film composers worldwide. |
| **George Gershwin** (1898‑1937) | Jazz/Classical crossover | “Rhapsody in Blue,” “An American in Paris.” Blended jazz idioms with orchestral forms. |
| **Duke Ellington** (1899‑1974) | Jazz | “Mood Indigo,” “It Don’t Mean a Thing (If It Ain’t Got That Swing).” A towering figure in big‑band jazz. |
| **Steve Reich** (born 1936) | Minimalism | “Music for 18 Musicians,” “Different Trains.” Known for phasing patterns and tape loops. |
| **John Adams** (born 1947) | Contemporary Classical | “Nixon in China,” “Short Ride in a Fast Machine.” Combines minimalism with lyrical elements. |
| **George Gershwin** (1898‑1937) | Jazz/Classical crossover | “Rhapsody in Blue,” “An American in Paris.” Blended jazz idioms with orchestral forms. |
| **Charles Ives** (1874‑1954) | Early 20th‑century | “The Unanswered Question,” “Concord Sonata.” Experimental use of polytonality and quotation. |
| **Samuel Barber** (1910‑1981) | Classical | “Adagio for Strings,” “Knoxville: Summer of 1915.” Known for lyrical, emotionally resonant works. |
| **John Cage** (1912‑1992) | Avant‑Garde | “4′33″,” prepared piano pieces. Introduced indeterminacy and silence into composition. |
| **Bobby McFerrin** (born 1950) | Vocal improvisation | “Don't Worry, Be Happy.” Known for acapella and vocal experimentation. |
| **Kurt Weill** (1900‑1950) | Musical theatre | “The Threepenny Opera,” “Three Waltzes.” Though German-born, he became a key figure in American musical theater. |

These names represent just a slice of the rich tapestry of American composition—from early experimentalists to modern film score maestros. If you’d like more detail on any particular composer or a deeper dive into a specific era or genre, let me know!
